title: The voice
hookLine: the adhan and Qur'an recited in maqams, melodic modes

cards: Two recordings of the same call to prayer. In the first, the muezzin's voice rises slowly, leans on one note, falls, and rises again, with something like an ache in it.
In the second, the voice is brighter and quicker, climbing in little steps. The words are the same in both, line for line. The tune is not.
Neither melody is written down as sheet music. They live in the throat, passed from teacher to student. Today, the last stop among the arts: the voice.

teach.b: Calligraphy, geometry, the vine, the dome, the garden, the carpet, the poem: the arts end where a Muslim day begins, with a voice. The Qur'an asks to be recited.

In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measure." And a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, tells people to beautify the Qur'an with their voices.
So there are rules, called tajwid: how long to hold a vowel, which letters press against each other, where to stop and where never to stop. Tajwid governs the sounds.
It doesn't fix the melody. Into that space come the maqamat, the melodic modes of Arab music, with names like bayati, hijaz, rast and saba.

Each has its own color; some listeners hear saba as sorrowful and hijaz as reaching. A skilled reciter may move from one mode to another as the verses shift, from warning to mercy, from story to promise.
Here Muslims differ, and fairly. Some scholars warn against reciting by musical rules, afraid the tune will start to bend the words. Others welcome the modes, as long as tajwid comes first.

teach.h: THE WORDS LEAD, THE VOICE SERVES.
teach.b: Both would say the words lead and the voice serves. The call to prayer works the same way: fixed words, and melodies that change from Cairo to Istanbul to Jakarta. No instrument.
Only a human voice, trained and offered to God. The voice is the art.

how: Muslims learn tajwid from teachers, often in mosque classes, and listen to celebrated reciters; muezzins in different cities call the same words of the adhan in their own local melodies.

o: a choir that sings hymns in a mosque on Fridays
the Prophet's own way of speaking, kept in hadith
the Qur'an and the call to prayer, sung with no instrument

p: a melodic mode, like hijaz or saba

s: the adhan has one official melody
the words are fixed; the melodies change from Cairo to Istanbul to Jakarta.
tajwid governs the sounds of recitation but not its melody
the rules cover vowels, letters and pauses; the modes color the tune.
all scholars welcome reciting in musical modes
some warn the tune may bend the words; others welcome it as long as tajwid comes first.

games.q: you're reciting, and the verses turn from warning to mercy. what does your voice do?
o: stay exactly as it was, no change.
move into another mode to match the meaning.
speed up to reach the end.
games.why: a skilled reciter may move between maqams as the meaning shifts, while keeping every rule of tajwid.

practice: Play a minute each of two adhans from different places, or, if you can't right now, listen to the room around you and to your own breath.

Don't follow the words; follow the shape: where the voice rises, where it holds, where it falls. If you pray, you can answer the call quietly, repeating its words after the muezzin; if you don't, just listen.

wordCard.voice: The voice. The Qur'an and the call to prayer, sung with no instrument, shaped by the rules of tajwid and colored by melodic modes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the voice is the art. Fixed words, and a living tune. That's the arts, done.
